question: Because the alpha helix and beta sheet are held by backbone hydrogen bonds rather than side chains, _____ can be formed by many unrelated amino acid sequences.
questions: Nearly half of human protein-coding genes contain long segments that never settle into any _____ at all, and those segments do real work.
In amyloid the sheets stack and pack against one another through their side chains, so a change of _____ is what turns a soluble protein into a fibril.
abstract:
The secondary structure of a protein is the regular arrangement its chain takes up over short stretches, and two forms are common: the alpha helix and the beta sheet, first proposed by Linus Pauling and Robert Corey in 1951. Both are held together by hydrogen bonds between the CO and NH groups of peptide bonds, in a helix between groups four residues apart, and in a sheet between two stretches of chain lying side by side, either parallel or running in opposite directions. The decisive point is that those bonds involve the backbone and not the side chains, so the same pattern can be formed by many unrelated sequences. A helix makes a complete turn every 3.6 amino acids, and both patterns were first found in ordinary material, the helix in the keratin of hair and the sheet in the fibroin of silk. Helices also wrap around one another into coiled-coils, which frame elongated proteins such as keratin and myosin, and a membrane protein usually crosses the lipid bilayer as a helix.

Not every part of a protein has any regular structure, and nearly half of human protein-coding genes contain long disordered segments that exist as shifting ensembles rather than fixed shapes. Those regions are not failures of folding, since they carry out signalling, transcriptional regulation, chromatin organisation and the assembly of organelles that have no membrane. Regular structure can also be built in the wrong way, and in an amyloid fibril beta sheets pack against one another through the side chains projecting from them, an arrangement called cross-beta packing. A single protein can take up several different amyloid folds, and those adopted by prion protein, tau, alpha-synuclein and TDP-43 differ from one neurodegenerative disease to another. Disordered regions remain among the hardest cases for structure prediction, whose methods principally return a single static conformation.
